source: REF·DB v1 (MAT_DOMAIN and MAT_DOM), in the plain style of the site

space.name: Space launch
space.d: NASA, ESA and commercial launch: performance first, cost tolerant, small production runs and qualification of each lot.
drivers: Mass is the main currency: each kilogram saved is payload gained
Compatibility with LOX, LH2 and LCH4 in cryogenic systems
Outgassing in vacuum, and long-duration thermal cycles
Fracture control of pressurised and rotating hardware (NASA-STD-5019)
Small lots make exotic alloys economic

defence.name: Defence and tactical
defence.d: Solid motors for defence: storage life first, mass produced, rugged, and subject to insensitive-munitions requirements.
drivers: A storage life of 10 to 20 years with no maintenance
A wide storage envelope, typically −54 to +71 °C (MIL-STD-810)
The insensitive-munitions response (STANAG 4439) drives the case and liner choice
Unit cost is important: production runs are large
Ruggedness in handling, transport and vibration

both.name: Both domains
both.d: Materials with an established history on both sides: usually the practical default.
drivers: A broad supply base with several qualified sources
Allowables well populated in MMPDS or CMH-17
Familiar to inspectors and stress authorities on both sides

ground.name: Ground and test equipment
ground.d: Test stands, ground support equipment, tooling and handling hardware: cost and availability govern, and mass is nearly unimportant.
drivers: Availability from stock is better than optimisation
Standard structural sections and stock sizes

Al-Li 2195: The alloy of the Shuttle External Tank and the SLS core barrel. Cryogenic tankage with a weight saving that pays only when mass is the currency. Friction stir welding is effectively mandatory.
Al 2219-T87: The classic weldable cryogenic tank alloy (Saturn, Shuttle, Delta). It keeps its toughness at LH2 temperature and it fusion welds, which Al-Li mostly does not.
Al-Li 2050 / 2099: Modern damage-tolerant Al-Li plate for machined launch-vehicle structure.
GRCop-42 (Cu-4Cr-2Nb): Developed by NASA for printed, regeneratively cooled chamber liners. A launch-vehicle material: no tactical motor is regeneratively cooled.
GRCop-84 (Cu-8Cr-4Nb): As GRCop-42. A bimetallic liner with a superalloy jacket.
NARloy-Z (Cu-3Ag-0.5Zr): The heritage SSME chamber liner, here for understanding legacy hardware.
NASA HR-1: Developed for turbomachinery in hydrogen and for regeneratively cooled nozzles.
JBK-75: Hydrogen turbopump housings. Cryogenic liquid propulsion only.
GRX-810 (NiCoCr ODS): NASA oxide-dispersion-strengthened superalloy for printed hot-section hardware. New, with a limited supply base.
C-103 Niobium (Nb-10Hf-1Ti): Radiation-cooled nozzle extensions on upper stages and in-space thrusters. It needs a silicide coating and a vacuum to work.
Rhenium (with Ir coating): Long-life apogee and station-keeping thrusters. Very expensive, with a constrained supply.
Iridium-coated rhenium: As above: satellite propulsion, not launch.
PICA (phenolic impregnated carbon): Heatshields for planetary entry and capsules.
AVCOAT 5026-39/HC-G: Heatshields of the Apollo and Orion crew capsules.
SLA-561V (cork/silicone): Backshells of planetary landers, and entry surfaces at low heat flux.
Reinforced carbon-carbon (RCC): Leading edges and nose caps of reusable spacecraft.
Alumina enhanced thermal barrier: Tile thermal protection of reusable spacecraft. Very low density and fragile: usable only where it is never handled in service and never sees rain or impact.
301 stainless (full hard): Large cryogenic tank structure on reusable launch vehicles: cheap, tough when cold, and work hardened to a useful strength.
304L / 316L (cryogenic): Cryogenic plumbing, dewars and vacuum jackets on launch and ground systems.
Invar 36 (FeNi36): Composite lay-up tooling and metering structures where dimensional stability governs.
Beryllium (S-200F): Optical benches and inertial platforms. The toxicity of machining it limits the supply base severely.
AlBeMet AM162 (Al-62Be): Satellite structure, optical mounts and guidance parts where specific stiffness governs. The beryllium brings controls on machining and a very narrow supply base.
M55J high-modulus carbon/epoxy: Satellite antenna booms and metering structures where stiffness, not strength, governs.
Zylon PBO/epoxy: Very light overwrap for composite pressure vessels. Creep and sensitivity to UV limit it to controlled environments.
SiC/SiC CMC: Reusable nozzle extensions and the next generation of turbine hardware.
ZrB2-SiC UHTC: Hypersonic leading edges and extreme throat inserts. A research-stage supply base.
D6AC (AMS 6431): The classic solid-motor case steel: high strength, deep hardening, proven in large defence motors. It needs tight control of the heat treatment and of hydrogen.
Maraging 18Ni-250: Motor cases where the simple heat treatment and the low distortion suit production quantities.
Maraging 18Ni-300: Higher-strength maraging steel for cases and highly loaded fittings.
AerMet 100: Ultra-high-strength landing gear and ballistic-tolerant fittings. Expensive.
300M: Landing gear and highly stressed shafts, with a long defence history.
HP 9-4-30: Weldable ultra-high-strength steel for fracture-critical structure.
EPDM insulation: Internal case insulation and stress-relief boots for solid motors.
EPDM insulation (silica filled): Silica-filled internal insulation for solid motors with a higher heat flux.
Carbon phenolic (ablative): Nozzle throat and entrance liners in both domains. The supply of the rayon precursor has long been a constraint.
Silica phenolic (ablative): Exit cone and housing insulation on solid motors.
Glass phenolic (ablative): Exit cone liners and blast tubes on solid motors. Cheaper than carbon phenolic and sufficient at lower heat flux, which is why it stays in production hardware.
Cork phenolic (Norcoat type): External insulation of stages and motors, and backshells of entry vehicles.
15CDV6 (1.7734): The European weldable case and pressure-vessel steel, at full strength as welded with no heat treatment after welding. Used in space and defence.
S-glass/epoxy: Filament-wound cases and radomes in both domains.
Aramid/epoxy (Kevlar): Damage-tolerant overwrap and containment. Kevlar-overwrapped cases have flown on both sides.
T800 carbon/epoxy: Filament-wound motor cases and pressure-vessel overwrap in both domains.
Carbon/epoxy (filament wound): The main modern case material in both domains.
S355 structural steel: Test stands, handling frames and baseplates. Never flight hardware.
4130 (25CrMo4): Test rigs, tube structure and ground hardware, and light flight structure.
Grey cast iron (EN-GJL-250): Machine bases and tooling. Not flight hardware.
Tool steel H13: Hot-work dies, extrusion tooling and the mandrels for winding composite cases. Tooling, not flight hardware, but tooling decides whether a flight part can be made at all.
Tool steel D2: Blanking and forming tools for sheet parts. A cold-work die steel and brittle, so never a structural part.
Tool steel O1: Gauges, jigs and fixtures where dimensional stability through the heat treatment is more important than strength.
Al 6082-T6: The UK default for general engineering and ground support equipment, and secondary flight structure.
9% Ni cryogenic steel: LNG and cryogenic storage on the ground. Seldom flight hardware.
